prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Due to the large amount of oil fume emissions, outdoor seating/display areas are strictly prohibited for this type of business to avoid affecting the road environment and reducing road quality, specifically including hotpot restaurants, barbecue restaurants, snack shops, etc. Figure 7.1-6 Schematic Diagram of
